d.title: Three norms, three different answers
d.caption: A norm is a choice, not a fact, and the choice changes which vector counts as “big”. For `[3, 4]` the three disagree — and the reason L1 produces sparse solutions is visible here: it charges the same for every unit of every coordinate.

d.title: Read the transformation off the columns
d.caption: Each column is where a basis vector lands, so the matrix can be read rather than multiplied out. The determinant is the area scale factor — and a **negative** one means the space was flipped, which is the detail people miss.

d.title: What a linear system can do
d.caption: Three outcomes and no others, decided by comparing the rank of the matrix with the rank of the augmented matrix and with the number of unknowns. “No solution” and “infinitely many” are both common in practice, which is why least squares exists.

d.title: What the eigenvalues tell you
d.caption: The signs decide the behaviour of everything built on the matrix — whether a quadratic has a minimum, whether a system is stable, whether a covariance matrix is usable. The **zero** row is the one that breaks code rather than merely degrading it.

d.title: SVD against eigendecomposition
d.caption: They are not alternatives for the same job. Eigendecomposition needs a square matrix and may not exist; the SVD exists for **every** matrix, which is why it is the one that underpins PCA, pseudoinverses and low-rank approximation.

columns.title: eigendecomposition
items: square matrices only
may not exist, and may be complex
A = Q Λ Q⁻¹ — the basis is not orthogonal in general
eigenvalues can be negative or complex
the right tool for powers of A and for dynamics

columns.title: SVD
items: ANY matrix, including rectangular
always exists, always real
A = U Σ Vᵀ — both bases orthonormal
singular values are real and non-negative, in order
the right tool for rank, pseudoinverse and compression

d.title: Centring is mandatory; scaling is a judgement
d.caption: Skip the centring and the first component points at the mean rather than at the spread — the result is not PCA at all. Scaling is a real decision: without it the component follows whichever feature has the largest units.

d.title: Which factorisation, and what it costs
d.caption: The cheap ones have conditions attached. Cholesky is twice as fast as LU and only works for a symmetric positive-definite matrix — so a failed Cholesky is itself a useful diagnostic that your matrix is not what you assumed.

d.title: The chain rule is the whole of backpropagation
d.caption: Differentiate the outside, keep the inside, multiply by the inside's derivative — then repeat. Backpropagation is this rule applied right to left so each factor is computed once, which is the only reason training a deep network is affordable.

items.label: name the composition
items.desc: y = f(g(h(x))) — write the layers out before differentiating

items.label: differentiate outermost, keep the inside
items.desc: f′(g(h(x))) — the argument does not change

items.label: multiply by the next derivative down
items.desc: × g′(h(x)) × h′(x) — a product of local slopes

items.label: right to left reuses every factor
items.desc: left to right recomputes them; this is forward against reverse mode

d.title: The gradient identities worth memorising
d.caption: Four results cover most of machine learning. The last is the one to hold onto: the gradient of a quadratic form is what makes least squares solvable in closed form, and it is where the normal equations come from.

d.title: What a schedule does to the step size
d.caption: The same budget of steps, spent differently. A constant rate cannot both move quickly early and settle late, which is the whole argument for a schedule — and warmup exists because the very first steps of a large model are the least trustworthy.

d.title: Which losses are convex, and why it matters
d.caption: Convexity buys one thing and it is a big one: every local minimum is global, so an optimiser that stops has found the answer. Neural networks give that up entirely, which is why their training is a search rather than a solve.
cells: any optimiser finds the global optimum

cells.text: restart it, and keep the best

d.title: The KKT conditions, in the order you check them
d.caption: Lagrange handles equalities; inequalities need the extra condition in step 4. **Complementary slackness** is the one that carries the meaning: a constraint either binds and has a positive multiplier, or is slack and its multiplier is zero.

items.label: stationarity
items.desc: the gradient of the Lagrangian is zero — the usual first-order condition

items.label: primal feasibility
items.desc: the original constraints hold at the point

items.label: dual feasibility
items.desc: the multipliers on inequalities are non-negative

items.label: complementary slackness
items.desc: μᵢgᵢ(x) = 0 — binding with μ>0, or slack with μ=0, never both

d.title: The finite-difference error has a floor
d.caption: Shrinking the step reduces truncation error and increases cancellation error, so the total has a minimum and then gets **worse**. The optimum for a forward difference is around the square root of machine epsilon — which is why automatic differentiation won.

d.title: Counting: two questions, four answers
d.caption: Every counting problem is one of these four, and the two questions are *does order matter* and *can an item repeat*. Choosing the wrong cell is the single commonest error in a probability interview — so decide the two questions before reaching for a formula.

d.title: PMF against PDF
d.caption: The distinction that causes the most confusion: a PMF **is** a probability, a PDF is not. A density can exceed 1 without contradiction because what must integrate to one is the area, not the height.

columns.title: PMF — discrete
items: P(X = x) is a probability, in [0, 1]
P(X = x) can be asked and answered
the values sum to 1
a bar chart with gaps

columns.title: PDF — continuous
items: f(x) is a DENSITY and may exceed 1
P(X = x) = 0 for every single x
the area under the curve is 1
probability comes from an interval, not a point

d.title: Everything from one coin flip
d.caption: Four distributions, one building block. Each answers a different question about the same repeated trial, which is why they are easy to confuse — the fix is to ask what is being counted and what is being held fixed.

d.title: The four continuous distributions, by the question they answer
d.caption: Each arises from a specific mechanism, and knowing the mechanism is what tells you whether it fits your data. The exponential's memorylessness is the property that most often makes it the wrong choice.
cells: no reason to prefer any value

cells.text: a sum of many small effects
waiting time at a constant rate

d.title: Bayes, and the term everyone drops
d.caption: The base rate is the term that gets forgotten, and it dominates the answer when the event is rare. A 99%-accurate test for a 1-in-10,000 condition still leaves a positive result far more likely to be a false alarm than a case.

items.label: the prior — P(H)
items.desc: the base rate, before any evidence. Dropping this is the classic error

items.label: the likelihood — P(E|H)
items.desc: how expected the evidence is if the hypothesis holds

items.label: the evidence — P(E)
items.desc: across ALL hypotheses, which is what normalises the result

items.label: the posterior — P(H|E)
items.desc: prior × likelihood ÷ evidence; now repeat with this as the prior

d.title: Simpson's paradox, with the numbers
d.caption: Treatment B wins in **both** groups and loses overall, because the groups differ in size and in severity. The lesson is not that statistics lies — it is that an aggregate without the confounder is a different question from the one you meant to ask.

d.title: Entropy, cross-entropy and KL
d.caption: Three quantities, one relationship: cross-entropy is entropy plus KL divergence. Training a classifier minimises cross-entropy, and because the data's own entropy is fixed, that is the same as minimising the KL divergence from the truth.

cells.text: the cost of coding p using q

cells: p is certain AND q = p

d.title: Three bounds, three prices
d.caption: Each buys tightness with an assumption. Markov needs almost nothing and tells you almost nothing; Hoeffding needs bounded variables and is the one that actually appears in practice.

d.title: Why the divisor is n − 1
d.caption: The sample mean is itself fitted from the data, so deviations are measured from a point chosen to make them small. Dividing by n therefore **understates** the spread; n − 1 corrects it, and the correction is exactly the degree of freedom the mean consumed.

items.label: the sample mean is estimated, not given
items.desc: it is placed where the squared deviations are smallest

items.label: so deviations from it are too small
items.desc: measured from the true mean they would be larger on average

items.label: dividing by n keeps that bias
items.desc: the expected value comes out as σ²(n−1)/n, not σ²

items.label: dividing by n − 1 removes it exactly
items.desc: unbiased for σ² — and this is Bessel's correction

d.title: The box plot's hidden rule
d.caption: The whiskers are **not** the minimum and maximum: they reach to the furthest point within 1.5 × IQR, and anything past that is drawn as an outlier. So a box plot is already making a judgement about your data before you read it.

items.label: outliers
items.sub: beyond 1.5 × IQR from the nearest quartile, drawn individually

items.label: upper whisker
items.sub: the furthest actual point WITHIN the fence — not the maximum

items.label: Q3
items.sub: 75th percentile — the top of the box

items.label: median
items.sub: the line inside the box, not the mean

items.label: lower whisker
items.sub: the furthest actual point within the lower fence

d.title: Kurtosis is about tails, not peaks
d.caption: The common description — “peakedness” — is wrong and leads people to misread it. Kurtosis is driven by the fourth power of deviations, so it is dominated by what happens far from the mean.

d.title: The four alternatives to causation
d.caption: Before claiming X causes Y, four other explanations have to be ruled out, and only the last is addressed by a bigger sample. This is the checklist that separates an analyst from a dashboard.
cells: ask how the data was collected

cells.text: more data — the ONLY one it fixes

d.title: Three distributions, routinely confused
d.caption: They answer different questions and only the third is what inference is about. The standard error shrinks with n; the population spread does not, which is the whole reason a large sample helps at all.

d.title: The four outcomes of a test
d.caption: α is chosen and β is a consequence of sample size and effect size. Note what the table does **not** contain: any probability that the null is true. A test conditions on the null, so it cannot report on it.

d.title: Four t-tests, four questions
d.caption: Picking the wrong one is usually a question about **pairing**: paired data analysed as independent throws away the pairing and loses power. Welch should be the default for two independent groups, because equal variance is an assumption you rarely have grounds for.
cells: is this mean equal to a fixed value?

d.title: What a p-value is, and what it is taken to be
d.caption: The definition is conditional on the null being **true**, which is exactly the thing people want it to tell them about. Everything in the right-hand column is a different quantity, and most of them require a prior to even state.

columns.title: what it is
items: P(data this extreme or more | H₀ is true)
a statement about the DATA, given an assumption
it conditions on the null, so it cannot judge it
0.04 and 0.06 are not different in kind
it says nothing about the size of the effect

columns.title: what it is read as
items: P(H₀ is true) — needs a prior; this is not it
the probability the result was a fluke
1 − p as the probability the effect is real
a measure of how big or important the effect is
a result that will replicate with probability 1 − p

d.title: Five misreadings, each with a number
d.caption: The middle column is what people infer; the right column is what is actually true. The last row is the one that costs most in practice — two studies either side of 0.05 are usually telling you the same thing.
cells: data this extreme is uncommon IF H₀ holds

cells.text: absence of evidence; check the power

cells: a tiny effect in a huge sample does this

d.title: Power is a four-way relationship
d.caption: Fix any three and the fourth follows. The practical reading is the bottom row: with a small true effect you need a large sample, and running the study anyway produces an underpowered result that cannot distinguish a small effect from none.
cells: time and money; power rises with √n

cells.text: it is a property of the world
more false positives — rarely worth it

d.title: Parametric against rank-based
d.caption: A rank test does not test the mean — it tests a shift in distribution, so the hypothesis changes with the method. That is the trade people forget: you buy robustness by answering a slightly different question.

d.title: Two error rates, two different jobs
d.caption: Controlling the family-wise rate asks that you make **no** false claims; controlling the false discovery rate asks that few of your claims be false. Which you want depends on whether a single false positive is expensive or merely inconvenient.

d.title: Credible against confidence
d.caption: They answer different questions, and the Bayesian one is the question people actually ask. The price is a prior, which has to be stated and defended rather than assumed away.

columns.title: 95% confidence interval
items: about the PROCEDURE: 95% of such intervals cover the parameter
the parameter is fixed; the interval is random
you may not say “95% chance it is in here”
needs no prior
the answer to a question nobody asked

columns.title: 95% credible interval
items: about THIS interval: 95% posterior probability the parameter is in it
the parameter has a distribution
you may say exactly what people want to say
needs a prior, stated explicitly
the answer to the question people mean

d.title: The order of operations for an experiment
d.caption: The order is the protection. Deciding the metric and the sample size **before** data arrives is what makes the resulting p-value mean anything — reverse any two of these steps and the analysis is exploratory, whatever it is called afterwards.

items.label: state the hypothesis and ONE primary metric
items.desc: secondary metrics are reported, never promoted after the fact

items.label: fix α, the MDE and the sample size
items.desc: power analysis decides the duration; the duration does not decide the power

items.label: check the randomisation actually worked
items.desc: sample ratio mismatch invalidates everything downstream

items.label: run to the planned n without looking
items.desc: or use a sequential method that was chosen in advance

items.label: analyse once, report the interval
items.desc: an effect size with its uncertainty, not a verdict

d.title: The regression assumptions, ranked by consequence
d.caption: They are not equally important, and treating them as a checklist of equals wastes effort. Independence and the right functional form change your conclusions; normality of residuals barely matters at any reasonable sample size.

cells.text: the model answers a different question

d.title: Multicollinearity: what it does and does not break
d.caption: It inflates the variance of the coefficients without biasing them, so prediction survives and interpretation does not. That asymmetry is the whole point: if you only need forecasts, a high VIF may be no problem at all.
cells: they trade off against each other

d.title: The review checklist, in the order it catches things
d.caption: Run top to bottom, because an early failure makes the later questions pointless. Most bad analyses die at the first two — how the data was collected, and what the comparison group actually is.

items.label: how was the data collected?
items.sub: selection and survivorship beat every later correction

items.label: what is the comparison group?
items.sub: no baseline means no effect to speak of

items.label: was the metric chosen before the data?
could a confounder explain it?
items.sub: name one and rule it out, or control for it

items.label: is the effect size worth acting on?
would it replicate?
items.sub: one study is a hypothesis, not a finding
